title: Walk while you have light (John 12:27–50)
hookLine: now is my soul troubled; walk while you have the light
tomorrow: he loved them to the end

cards: Late afternoon light goes gold and long, and there's maybe an hour before dark. Anything you meant to do outside, you'd better do now. Farmers know it; kids playing in the street know it.
Today's passage is the late afternoon of Jesus's public life in John's Gospel. After this, he won't speak to the crowds again.
Everything from chapter thirteen on happens in private, with his closest friends, and then on the way to the cross. These are his last public words. And he begins by admitting something.

teach.b: "Now is my soul troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour: but for this cause came I unto this hour." He's troubled, and says so.
The other Gospels show it in the garden of Gethsemane; John shows it here. And instead of asking to be spared, he prays: "Father, glorify thy name."
Then a voice comes from heaven: "I have both glorified it, and will glorify it again." The crowd hears it differently. Some say it thundered.
Others say an angel spoke. The same sound, and people hear what they're ready to hear. Then he says, "And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me."
Lifted up: on a cross, and, as John hears it, into glory, both at once.
Then comes today's line, with the urgency of sunset: "Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you." It's not a threat.

It's what someone says to a friend when the sun is going down: don't wait. "While ye have light, believe in the light, that ye may be the children of light." Then, John says, he went away and hid himself.

teach.h: NOT TO JUDGE, BUT TO SAVE.
teach.b: Before the curtain falls on the public ministry, Jesus cries out a summary of everything he's said, and it ends gently: he came not to judge the world, but to save the world.

teach.h: WALK WHILE YE HAVE THE LIGHT.
teach.b: Some readers call John chapters one to twelve the Book of Signs. Tomorrow, a new part begins.

how: Christians often read this passage in Holy Week; some pray at sunset, keeping the evening as a time to remember the light while it lasts.

games.q: your soul is troubled, and the hour you've dreaded has come. what do you pray?
games.why: he names the first prayer and sets it aside: "for this cause came I unto this hour. Father, glorify thy name."

practice: Notice today's light: is it morning, noon, already going down?

Think of one good thing you've been putting off, a call to an aging parent, an apology, a thank-you note, a visit, something that won't wait forever, and notice any reluctance, and how small it is next to the thing itself.
If you pray, ask for help to do it; if not, simply choose the hour for it.

wordCard.voice: Gethsemane. The garden where the other Gospels show Jesus's trouble of soul; John shows that same trouble here instead, in his last public words.
